questionText: Consider a process P running on a CPU. Which one or more of the following events will always trigger a context switch by the OS that results in process P moving to a non-running state (e.g., ready, blocked)?
options: P makes a blocking system call to read a block of data from the disk
P tries to access a page that is in the swap space, triggering a page fault
An interrupt is raised by the disk to deliver data requested by some other process
A timer interrupt is raised by the hardware
explanation:
Option (A): When process $P$ makes a blocking system call, it cannot proceed until the requested I/O operation finishes. The OS transitions process $P$ to the blocked state and performs a context switch to run another process. Thus, this event always results in $P$ moving to a non-running state.

Option (B): Accessing a page in the swap space causes a page fault. The OS must fetch the required page from disk (an I/O operation), forcing process $P$ into the blocked state while waiting for the page to load. Therefore, this event always causes $P$ to move to a non-running state.

Option (C): When an interrupt is raised for another process, the CPU temporarily executes the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR). Once the ISR completes, the scheduler may decide to resume process $P$ directly without transitioning $P$ to a non-running state.

Option (D): A timer interrupt triggers the scheduler, but if process $P$ is the only runnable process or has higher priority, the OS may immediately reschedule process $P$ to continue execution without moving it to the ready state.

Hence, options A and B are correct.
